title: They Tried to Bury Main Vaapas Aaunga. Eight Days Later, It's Pulling a Queen.
excerpt: Imtiaz Ali's Diljit Dosanjh drama opened to a disastrous ₹1.28 crore and an 'anti-national' pile-on. Its second Saturday just became the biggest day of its run — and trade calls it miraculous.
body:
Two weeks ago, **Main Vaapas Aaunga** looked finished. **Imtiaz Ali**'s Diljit Dosanjh-led drama opened on June 12 to a frankly disastrous ₹1.28 crore — the kind of number that empties screens by Monday and sends a film quietly to streaming with its tail between its legs. Add the "anti-national" pile-on it walked into for daring to imagine a Pakistan without cartoon villains, and the obituaries were halfway written.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=PRUTWluKRW8</youtube>

Then something happened that almost never happens anymore.

https://x.com/vikkisingh46711/status/2068544302972842304

The film refused to die. By its second Saturday — yesterday — collections more than doubled to ₹4.45 crore, the single biggest day of its entire run, *eight days after release*. Trade circles, normally allergic to the word, are calling it miraculous. And they are reaching for one name to describe it.

> "With Main Vaapas Aaunga, we are evidencing something that hasn't happened for as long as I can remember... One film that I can remember following such trajectory was Kangana Ranaut's Queen." — Bollywood Hungama box office desk

That comparison carries weight. **Queen**, back in 2014, opened at ₹1.75 crore and clawed its way to a ₹61 crore cult-classic lifetime — roughly 35 times its first day. Pure, unbuyable word of mouth. The kind of run that turns a film into a thing people *insist* you watch. Main Vaapas Aaunga is now walking that exact tightrope, and it's further along than Queen was at the same stage.

Look at the trajectory and it reads like a heartbeat coming back. Day one: ₹1.28 crore, near-dead. Day two: a sub-par ₹1.85 crore. Day three: an ordinary ₹2.50 crore. Then, on day seven — a Thursday, of all the lifeless slots — the number jumped to ₹2.28 crore, nearly matching its opening Sunday. Distributors noticed. Exhibitors noticed. And so, even as the much bigger **Cocktail 2** stormed in to grab screens, Main Vaapas Aaunga held its shows. Second Friday stayed steady at ₹2 crore. Second Saturday exploded.

For context on how rare this is: Queen's best single day was ₹4.85 crore on its second Sunday. Main Vaapas Aaunga is projected to cross ₹6 crore today. It has already pulled its total to ₹18.91 crore — modest on paper, but climbing in a direction films simply do not climb in 2026, when most titles lose 50% by their second Friday and vanish by week two.

So what flipped? The answer is the part the early outrage missed. **A.R. Rahman**'s score — quiet, aching, unmistakably his — became the film's slow-burn engine, with the track *Tere Paas Main* doing the heavy lifting on social media long after the trolls moved on. Imtiaz Ali, a filmmaker who has always trusted longing over loudness, made the kind of movie that doesn't sell out a Friday but ruins you by a Tuesday and sends you texting three friends. And **Diljit Dosanjh**, fresh off a global touring high, is giving the performance people are now telling each other not to miss.

There's a sweeter irony underneath. The controversy that was supposed to sink it — the accusation that a Punjabi star and a Muslim composer had made something insufficiently patriotic — appears to have done the opposite. The noise put the film in front of people who then actually watched it, and what they found wasn't a manifesto. It was a love story about distance, return, and the ache of belonging to a place you keep leaving. Which, if you think about it, is the most diaspora story imaginable.

And that's exactly why this one matters across the oceans. For NRIs in the US, UK and Canada — people who know intimately what *main vaapas aaunga*, "I will come back," actually costs — this is the rare film built for the feeling rather than the franchise. It's still in select overseas theatres on the strength of this turnaround, and an OTT landing is expected within weeks once the theatrical run cools; watch for it on a major streamer, with Rahman's soundtrack already on every platform for the impatient.

Here's the sharp take: in a year of ₹1,000-crore spy universes and mythological gods, the most interesting story at the Indian box office is a small, "failed" film that nobody can kill. If it holds its weekdays, Main Vaapas Aaunga won't just survive — it'll become the thing people brag about having seen early. The trolls handed it the spotlight. The audience is deciding to keep it there.
